experiment.name: phase2_tier2_covert
_comment: Tier 2: the receiver reads world-readable scaling_cur_freq and holds no
privilege of any kind. This is the run the security claim rests on --
tier 1 needs root, and root can already read the victim's memory.
Config-B is mandatory. Config-A pins the frequency precisely to remove
the DVFS response this receiver lives on, so the same experiment under
Config-A decodes a flat line by construction.
Ten victim threads across the P-cores, not the four used everywhere in
Phase 1. The feasibility sweep found four threads move the frequency only
-195 MHz with a CI that barely excludes zero, while ten move it -804 MHz:
the channel exists only once enough of the part is loaded that something
has to limit. That is a real precondition of the attack and is reported
as one rather than hidden in a default.
Symbol periods are an order of magnitude longer than tier 1's. The RAPL
counter updates about every millisecond; the governor's pstate decisions
are far slower, and the response being observed is a control loop rather
than an instantaneous quantity. 32-256 ms is a guess at the usable range
and the sweep exists to replace it with a measurement.
The receiver watches two CPUs: core 0, its own, and core 2, a victim's.
An attacker need not know where the victim runs, so which of those
decodes is worth knowing. Read the second with --freq-column 1.
A single smoke run (results/20260903-141103) decoded 256 ms symbols at
BER 0.19 -- 6 errors in 32 bits, which beats chance at p about 7e-4 --
while its A/A sat at 0.56 with the sync landing 9.6 chips from anything.
That is one run, and the feasibility sweep's mean-difference proxy found
no frequency effect above its own control at any load, so the two
readings have to be reconciled by repeats rather than by choosing one.
This sweep exists to decide it.
aa_256ms is the control, at the same load and rate as the row that
carried the smoke result.
